genre: opinion essay (a newspaper column): a city painting its grey footbridges in bright colours

versions.text:
For fifty years before this summer, the seven footbridges over the Askel were the colour of wet pavement. Now they are saffron, coral, teal, plum, lime, sky blue and tangerine. Residents voted online last spring to paint them, but the colours came from a class at Larch Street School, and Councillor Mara Varga carried the class's scheme to the council, which adopted it whole on the children's promise that people would find the right bridge at last.

The thinking behind that scheme is worth following step by step. Each bridge now wears the colour of the bus line that stops at its far end, so a commuter on the station steps can pick out her bridge by finding her bus's colour across the water. In 2019 the city planned to paint every bridge the same green; the children saw that seven matching bridges would be as hard to tell apart as the grey ones had been before. It is the cleverest piece of public design this city has produced in my lifetime, and it was drawn by eleven-year-olds.

The parks crew earned their share of the credit. Working from the class's chart, they painted between midnight and dawn so that every bridge stayed open, and before a brush touched the concrete they repaired each crack the inspectors had ringed in coloured chalk that spring, at a cost the council had set aside years ago. At the class's request they fixed boxes to the railings as well, and stock now blooms along all seven spans.

There was one mix-up, when the depot misread an order and sent the coral tins to the wrong bridge, and a wet July slowed the work, since paint will not take on concrete in the rain. Visitors now come down to the river to photograph the spans, but the real test comes at eight each morning, when commuters stream off the trains and cross to their buses without a second look.

The class deserves to see its scheme on every bridge Pellam builds from now on, and the crew has earned the thanks of everyone who crosses the Askel on the way to work.

For fifty years before this summer, the seven footbridges over the Askel were the colour of wet pavement. Now they are saffron, coral, teal, plum, lime, sky blue and tangerine, colours Councillor Mara Varga picked herself from a paint card in her office. A class at Larch Street School had sent the council a careful scheme matching each bridge to a bus line, so that commuters could tell the bridges apart and find the right one, and it went into a drawer.

What the bridges needed this summer was repair, not paint. Every spring the city's inspectors ring cracks in coloured chalk, yellow for watch and red for mend, and this April the railings of the plum and teal bridges carried eleven red rings. Those repairs, already logged by the inspectors, were put off to next year, and the parks crew's orders were to paint straight over the chalk. Residents had asked in an online vote for the railings to come first.

The paint came from Holm & Daughters, whose stock rose on the exchange the week the order was announced. The whole bill came to a third of the cost of mending the cracks, and the council signed it off in a single evening. Visitors have since come down to the river to photograph the spans, a side effect Councillor Varga now mentions in every interview.

The crew can hardly be blamed. They worked fast, losing a day to a mix-up at the depot, which misread an order and sent the coral tins to the wrong bridge, and a few more to rain on the bare concrete. In 2019 the city planned to paint every bridge the same green, and that plan was shelved for want of money; this one found its money by taking it from the railings.

The city should have mended the railings in the spring and painted the bridges next year, in whatever colours its residents and its schoolchildren chose. Instead it has put a bright coat over eleven red rings and called the job finished.

For fifty years before this summer, the seven footbridges over the Askel were the colour of wet pavement. Now they are saffron, coral, teal, plum, lime, sky blue and tangerine. Residents voted online for paint, the parks crew chose the seven colours themselves, and Councillor Mara Varga persuaded the council to buy a thick sealing paint, the kind used on harbour walls, for concrete that has been soaking up rain since 1971.

It helps to know how the bridges are checked. Each spring the city's inspectors walk every span and read the bare concrete for hairline cracks, which show as thin dark lines after rain, and they ring each one in coloured chalk. A crack caught before water gets in is a cheap repair; mending the cracks found late has cost the city far more. The whole method depends on seeing the grey surface itself.

So far the bridges are busier than they have been in years. Visitors come down to the river with cameras, and Mr. Abeyta at the foot of the teal bridge now simmers a second pot of stock each morning for the crowds. A class at Larch Street School had sent in a scheme matching each bridge to a bus line, so that people could tell the bridges apart and find the right one, but the crew picked colours that would show from the station. A mix-up at the depot, which misread an order and sent the coral tins to the wrong bridge, held up the work for a day.

What I cannot stop thinking about is next April. The sealing paint is thick and glossy, so the inspectors will be reading colour instead of concrete, and a crack that opens under the coat this winter could stay out of sight until it has run through a railing. In 2019 the city planned to paint every bridge the same green, and that plan was shelved for want of money.

I will be on the plum bridge when the inspectors come next spring, waiting with my stomach in a knot to see whether they can still find what the new coat may be hiding from them.

For fifty years before this summer, the seven footbridges over the Askel were the colour of wet pavement. Now they are saffron, coral, teal, plum, lime, sky blue and tangerine, the seven colours that won an online vote of residents in the spring. Councillor Mara Varga ran the vote, and the parks crew painted to its results over six weeks.

I knew those bridges before any of this. On winter mornings the grey spans vanished into the river mist, so that walkers seemed to step off the bank into nothing, and on summer nights the concrete held the day's heat long after dark while we sat on the railings. Every spring the inspectors ringed the cracks in coloured chalk, and by June the rain had washed the rings into pale clouds we traced with our fingers. That grey went under the first coat of saffron in July, and the bridges I grew up on went with it.

I come of ferry stock: my grandfather rowed passengers across the Askel until the bridges opened in 1971, and he walked the grey spans every evening of his retirement. The council's leaflet for the project showed the riverbank crowded with visitors holding cameras, and on weekends now they come.

Other plans came and went first. A class at Larch Street School once put forward a scheme matching each bridge to a bus line, so that people could find the right bridge, and in 2019 the city meant to paint every bridge the same green; the vote overtook both. The crew lost a day when the depot misread an order in a mix-up over the coral tins, and they repaired the cracks the inspectors had ringed, at a cost set aside long ago, before any paint went on.

People say the bridges are easier to tell apart now. What I miss is the hour when all seven turned grey together in the dusk and the river seemed to carry them away, and that hour will not come back.

For fifty years before this summer, the seven footbridges over the Askel were the colour of wet pavement. In May the council ordered enough paint to give all seven the same green, and they came out saffron, coral, teal, plum, lime, sky blue and tangerine.

Here is how it happened. Every spring the city's inspectors mark each bridge with a dab of coloured chalk, a different colour for each span, so that their reports can name a bridge by colour instead of a number; they also ring any cracks they find. The work order told the parks crew to paint each bridge in its marked colour, meaning the green swatch clipped to the order. The crew found seven dabs of chalk and matched every one, sending to the depot for the extra shades as they went.

By the time anyone looked at the order again, four bridges were finished and people were stopping on them to stare. The bronze sentry who has stood at the middle of the lime bridge since 1971 now rests his hand on a rifle with a tangerine stock, because an inspector once tagged the gun instead of the railing. I grin every time I cross that bridge and see him standing guard in his new colours.

When the mix-up came to light, residents phoned all week asking to keep the colours, and Councillor Mara Varga's online vote to name the bridges was won easily by Plum, Lime, Teal and the rest. A class at Larch Street School has since worked out that the colours nearly match the bus lines at the far ends, so people can tell the bridges apart and find the right one, and the class now explains its scheme to visitors who come down to the river. The two cracks the inspectors had ringed were repaired first, at no extra cost, and a week of rain only delayed the paint on the concrete.

Of all the stories this city tells about itself, this is the one I most enjoy: seven bridges painted the colours of a box of chalk because one line of a work order was followed exactly as written.
